source.notes: A decommissioned AlphaGo backend rack, photographed 6 January 2025 on display with its AlphaGo nameplate, uploaded to Commons under CC0. Where it is displayed is not stated on the file page. Hung as a branch beside the replayed game.

object.description: One rack of the machine that played. The AlphaGo that beat Lee Sedol ran across Google's data centres on 1,920 processors and 280 graphics chips, and on a new kind of chip, the tensor processing unit, which Google had built in secret for exactly this sort of arithmetic and announced two months after the match. A later AlphaGo Zero needed only four of them. This is a retired rack, kept and labelled.
facts: The match version used 48 TPUs; the program had been trained on thirty million positions from human games and then on games against itself.
Lee Sedol took the one game in five by finding a move the machine had thought one in ten thousand.
DeepMind retired AlphaGo from competition in 2017 after beating the world number one, Ke Jie, three games to none.
